title: The Treasury Secretary Trades the Bond Market Like a Position, and Prices Will Win
dek: US Treasury Secretary Bessent is intervening in the bond market, trade and sanctions with a trader's mindset, but inflation and deficits keep pushing prices up, and his strategy may come to nothing.
why: A deep dive into Bessent's multi-front interventions and their internal contradictions, uniquely valuable for understanding the US fiscal and market game.
who: Investors, policy analysts and financial journalists watching US fiscal policy, the Treasury market and macroeconomic maneuvering.
skip: The opening recap of Bessent's career can be skipped; go straight to the intervention details.

points.h: The Treasury secretary runs debt management as a trading position
points.body: Bessent treats Treasury debt management as a trading position rather than a traditional neutral operation. He judges that the market has mispriced the 10-year yield and bets that long-term rates will fall. To that end, he shortens the debt's duration by buying back long bonds and issuing short bills, pushing long-term yields down. If he is right, the government can refinance at lower rates; if he is wrong, it must keep rolling short-term debt at market rates, a huge risk.

points.h: Pushing yields down is the same as switching off the deficit alarm
points.body: Druckenmiller wrote in The Wall Street Journal that Bessent's buybacks are not liquidity management but an attempt to change a number the government does not like. He noted there is no sign of market failure, and that rising yields are a true reflection of inflation, deficits and debt. Suppressing yields is the same as switching off the alarm that forces politicians to deal with the deficit; every basis point is a subsidy for delay.

points.h: Bond yields are arithmetic, and armies cannot take them down
points.body: Trump hinted that high rates might be solved by military means, and Bessent did not deny it when asked whether he had directed intervention in the bond market. Boyle joked that he does not know how an army would intervene in bond yields, but noted that when all economic tools fail, the military becomes the last option. Yet yields are an arithmetic result; they cannot be invaded or blockaded.

points.h: A tariff war and lower long-term yields cannot both succeed
points.body: Tariffs on Canada are ultimately borne by US consumers, raising production costs and prices. Rising inflation leads bond investors to demand higher yields, running directly counter to Bessent's effort to push long-term yields down. The trade war and the bond-market intervention contradict each other, like stepping on the gas while pulling the handbrake.

points.h: Without daring to sanction China, pressure on Iran is empty talk
points.body: Bessent previewed an "economic D-Day" against Iran, but in the end only sanctioned about 60 entities, naming no country or deadline. Because China buys about 90% of Iran's crude oil, real pressure would require sanctioning China, but Trump is about to meet with Xi Jinping, making it politically unworkable. Iranian negotiators openly mocked the US bluff.

points.h: Stablecoins are both a sanctions loophole and a buyer of short bills
points.body: The government sanctions Iran on one hand while promoting cryptocurrency on the other, and Iran is using crypto to evade sanctions. Bessent expects the stablecoin market to grow to $2 trillion, creating demand for short-term Treasuries and supporting his buyback strategy. This creates the awkward situation of depending on the very channel the enemy uses.

points.h: Warsh hints at a rate hike, exactly the opposite of the Treasury secretary's bet
points.body: New Fed Chair Warsh said at Jackson Hole that inflation has exceeded target for 65 consecutive months and that financial conditions are not restrictive, hinting at a possible rate hike. Market expectations for a September hike rose from 35% to 60%. Warsh and Bessent disagree: one sees high yields as the problem, the other sees them as a signal.

points.h: A third of Treasuries mature within a year, a bet on rate cuts
points.body: About one-third of marketable Treasuries mature within 12 months, and financing them with short-term bills is a bet that future rates will fall. If Warsh hikes, the maturity wall will push interest costs higher. Bessent's "333" plan (deficit down to 3% of GDP, 3% growth, 3% more energy production) has gone off track, with growth at only 1.5%-2% and the deficit about twice the target.
